title: Dai Viet land-unit visual direction: early Ly through later Tran
scope: Historical art direction for unit pilots only. Keep stock skeletons, weapon class, animation, and gameplay identity. No Berber files/assets referenced or reused.

period.note: Museum pages use 1225 in dynasty narrative and 1226 in exhibition title; retain those source labels rather than force a single transition date.

source_supported_observations.claim: The Vietnam National Museum of History summarizes Ly-Tran rule, military history, and the Ly/Tran sequence; it describes three victories over Mongol forces and dates the period 1009-1400.

The museum describes a Tran terracotta military-officer figure, 13th-14th century, standing upright in a lion-face hat; the torso is decorated with lozenge and bodhi-leaf forms. It is a roof-ridge decorative figure, not a preserved uniform or direct portrait of field kit.

The museum's Ly-Tran brown-ceramic article says figures of spearmen are shown exercising/fighting or hunting with sword and shield; it also describes an elephant-shaped Tran ewer with a driver and small Tran human heads with hair bound in a turban.

The museum article distinguishes Ly lotus decoration with raised, more elaborate petals from Tran style with flatter petals and rounded tips. These are ceramic dating/design observations, not evidence of clothing patterns.
The Ho Chi Minh City History Museum's Tran-Ho room page describes an organized army, agriculture/industry/commerce, and the Tran-era resistance; its pictured objects on that page are ceramics.

art_direction_from_user: substantial stock-donor clothing/equipment remodel while preserving skeletons, weapon class, and animation
design_language.evidence_boundary: The museum material consulted documents ceramics, small terracotta figures, motifs, and broad military context. It does not establish surviving Ly-Tran textile uniforms, rattan armor, bamboo armor, specific unit headgear, or the proposed material palette. Those are visual interpretations for production, not historical fact claims.
design_language.early_to_later_progression: Early-Ly treatment: cleaner cloth shapes and selective raised/pointed lotus bands on small trim. Later-Tran treatment: more visibly martial layering and flatter rounded lotus bands. Apply motif evolution as an art cue inferred from ceramic decoration; do not present it as a documented clothing chronology.
shape_and_material_rules: Read large garment and armor masses at gameplay distance; use a few broad weave bands, not noisy micro-weave.
Keep rattan/bamboo shapes irregular and worn, cloth matte, iron dark and low-gloss; bronze should remain limited to tiny fittings/player accents.
Do not apply the lion-face hat to ordinary troops; reserve it for a command/ceremonial variant if the unit set needs a distinct officer cue, and mark that use as interpretation.

pilot_directions.silhouette: Retain donor head/limb proportions, bow, quiver, hand poses, and animation. Widen the torso vest only about 5-8% at ribs/shoulders; end it just above the hip crease. Keep one clear center overlap/opening. Add a single shallow oval or rounded-rectangle back shield on two diagonal straps, shoulder blades to belt, placed clear of bowstring and quiver.
pilot_directions.headgear: Simple tied cloth wrap or soft close cap; no tall helmet. This is an art choice, not established by the cited artifacts.
pilot_directions.clothing_equipment: Dark cloth sleeved tunic under a coarse rattan/cane vest with a few broad horizontal courses and visible diagonal ties; shallow back shield; stock bow and quiver remain readable. Restrained bronze only at a few fasteners/player accents.
pilot_directions.evidence: Museum describes ceramic spearmen with sword and shield, not archers, bows, rattan armor, back shields, or this garment cut. The vest/back-shield requirements are user-approved art direction; all specific construction is interpretation.
pilot_directions.proportion_note: Keep vest thickness visually shallow; use broad plates/ribs at torso scale, avoid changing shoulder silhouette enough to clip bow draw or stock animations.

pilot_directions.silhouette: Keep donor spear length, grip, and stance. Add a lightly armored broad shoulder/upper-torso layer over a knee-length split tunic; define a compact waist tie and a small forearm wrap without enlarging hands or changing weapon reach.
pilot_directions.headgear: Low cloth wrap/close cap for regular rank; the lion-face hat is documented only on the small terracotta roof-ridge officer figure and should not become a generic helmet.
pilot_directions.clothing_equipment: Layered cloth with a limited rattan/bamboo chest panel, dark-iron fittings, and one small shield only if donor equipment supports it; keep spear as the clear class read. Ly raised lotus / Tran flat rounded-petal trim can distinguish phase subtly.
pilot_directions.evidence: Sword-and-shield-bearing spearmen are described on Ly-Tran ceramics. Specific armor, hat, split tunic, forearm wrap, rattan and spear treatment are interpretations; the cited museum wording does not identify the figure as a spear-bearing infantryman.

pilot_directions.silhouette: Practical, lightly fitted long-sleeved or rolled-sleeve tunic with side vents above the knee, narrow tied waist, straight trousers, simple sandals or bare feet per donor; vary hem, sleeve roll, and cloth bundle while preserving donor proportions and tools.
pilot_directions.headgear: Optional tied cloth headband or bare head; source does not establish village headwear.
pilot_directions.clothing_equipment: Matte worn natural cloth, small bamboo/rattan carrying basket or tool binding where compatible with stock props; no uniform armor. Bronze accents omitted or nearly absent.
pilot_directions.evidence: No cited artifact documents the proposed male civilian outfit. This is practical visual interpretation consistent with the user's request for varied civilians; costume pieces must not be labeled as sourced historical dress.

pilot_directions.silhouette: Keep the donor female body and animation. Use a wrapped or cross-over upper tunic with rolled/short sleeves, tied waist, and an ankle-to-calf lower wrap or skirt over fitted trousers; keep the outline work-ready and vary hems and sleeve length across variants.
pilot_directions.headgear: Optional cloth wrap or hair tied back; both are interpretation in this brief.
pilot_directions.clothing_equipment: Worn natural cloth, simple waist pouch or shallow basket if stock-compatible; no armor and no courtly jewelry. Keep the skirt/wrap clear of locomotion and tool animations.
pilot_directions.evidence: The cited museums provide no clothing evidence for Ly-Tran female villagers. This is a production interpretation only.

pilot_directions.silhouette: Keep stock horse body, rider scale, saddle pose, weapon, and animation. Give rider a short split riding tunic, tied waist, compact shoulder/torso protection, and close head wrap so the mounted silhouette stays distinct from foot spearmen.
pilot_directions.headgear: Close wrap or low cap; no documented mounted-warrior headgear in the consulted museum sources.
pilot_directions.clothing_equipment: Layered cloth with restrained cane/rattan reinforcing panels; dark iron fittings, small bronze accents; preserve the donor saddle/tack and weapon class. Avoid inventing a highly ornate barded horse unless the donor already has it.
pilot_directions.evidence: Museum sources support Tran-era military context and horse imagery among ceramic animal motifs, but not the proposed mounted uniform, armor, tack, or specific horse-warrior kit. All garment and equipment details are interpretation.

pilot_directions.silhouette: Retain stock elephant anatomy, proportions, gait, and all attachment points. Keep any rider/mahout low and close to the neck/back so the animal remains the dominant silhouette.
pilot_directions.headgear: For a mahout, use a simple tied cloth wrap or close cap as interpretation; do not copy the lion-face officer roof figure onto the handler.
pilot_directions.clothing_equipment: Simple cloth saddle cloth and rope/cane harness with limited dark-iron fittings; use a restrained Ly/Tran lotus band as surface decoration. Preserve stock functional equipment and animation.
pilot_directions.evidence: The museum describes a Tran elephant-shaped ceramic ewer with driver and an elephant-driver figurine. These support an elephant-and-driver motif, not actual war-elephant armor, harness, saddle cloth, or the proposed rider clothing.

pilot_directions.silhouette: Keep the selected stock siege unit's frame, crew count, weapon, and attack/read animation. Add broad wood beams, visible rope/lashing joints, and a few dark-iron brackets; do not add weapon mechanisms or extra moving parts that alter the class read.
pilot_directions.headgear: Crew use simple cloth wraps/caps as an art interpretation; preserve donor faces and animation.
pilot_directions.clothing_equipment: Worn cloth with limited protective panels for crew; weathered timber and rope are the proposed natural-material language. Identify the actual stock siege donor before modeling so no machine type is inferred from the museum sources.
pilot_directions.evidence: No cited museum source establishes this siege-engine design or its crew clothing. All forms in this direction are production interpretation; only the broad Tran military context is documented.

guardrails: No change to skeletons, weapon class, attack timing, or animation.
Avoid presenting the proposed outfits, rattan armor, bamboo armor, or colors as documented historical fact.
Keep military protection varied by role; civilian pilots remain visibly practical and unarmored.
Use the exact selected donor resource and actual skeleton/animation contracts during integration; this brief does not nominate asset IDs.
